cards.title: Mark Bergsma
cards.prompt: Wikimedia ran a top-ten website on donations, out of three data centres. Which one ran the application, what ran in the other two, and how many people and dollars a year was the whole plant?
cards.answer: Mark Bergsma documented it. Tampa, Florida was the primary cluster and the only one with application servers; Amsterdam and Seoul were caching-only. About 350 servers run by roughly 6 people, a foundation of 9 employees on around $2M a year, mostly donations.
cards.body: Mark Bergsma, Wikimedia Foundation. His architecture deck: “3 data centers: Tampa, Amsterdam, Seoul” — “Primary cluster in Tampa, Florida”, “Secondary caching-only clusters in Amsterdam, the Netherlands and Seoul, South Korea”. 350 servers, “...managed by ~ 6 people”, 9 employees, “Yearly budget of around $2M, supported mostly through donations”.

cards.title: MediaWiki, includes/OutputPage.php
cards.prompt: MediaWiki decides in one condition whether a page may live at the edge. What is the condition, and which response header does it always send so no cache downstream can get that decision wrong?
cards.answer: The condition is the absence of the PHP session cookie: no cookie and the page goes to Squid with an s-maxage; cookie present and it goes out Cache-Control: private, must-revalidate, max-age=0. Every response carries Vary: Accept-Encoding, Cookie.
cards.body: sendCacheControl() emits “Vary: Accept-Encoding, Cookie” under the comment “maintain different caches for logged-in users and non-logged in ones”, and hands Squid an s-maxage only when the session cookie is absent. Otherwise: “Cache-Control: private, must-revalidate, max-age=0”. The cache key was decided in the application, not the CDN config.

cards.title: RFC 2756 — HTCP
cards.prompt: An edit has to un-publish one URL from every cache on three continents within seconds, and TTLs cannot do it. Which published protocol carries that order, and what is the op-code called?
cards.answer: HTCP, the Hyper Text Caching Protocol, RFC 2756 (Vixie and Wessels, January 2000). The op-code is CLR. Wikimedia sent one UDP multicast CLR per edited URL to every Squid at once.
cards.body: “Hyper Text Caching Protocol (HTCP/0.0)”, P. Vixie and D. Wessels, January 2000. Its CLR op-code, in full: “Tell a cache to completely forget about an entity. RD is honoured.” Wikimedia rejected expiry times for wiki pages; on each edit the application servers multicast one HTCP message naming the URL.

cards.title: The one image server
cards.prompt: Wikimedia split its Squid caches into two groups, Text and Media. One of them hit 98%, the best number in the deck. Which one, what was sitting behind it as the origin, and what does a hit rate that high let a team get away with?
cards.answer: Media — images and other large static files; Text was wiki pages, at 85%. Behind Media sat a single image server: 1.3 TB, 4 million files, overloaded at 100 requests/s, uploads over NFS mounted on every application server, backups taking about two weeks. A 98% hit rate keeps an origin alive that could not otherwise ship.
cards.body: Behind the 98%: “1 Image server containing 1.3 TB of data, 4 million files”, “Overloaded serving just 100 requests/s”, uploads over NFS mounted on all application servers, “Not scalable”, “Backups take ~ 2 weeks”. The cache was not making that origin better. It was making it survivable.

cards.title: The cache got a veto
cards.prompt: Twenty years after those Amsterdam racks, what is still true of Wikimedia's topology, and what did the caching tier permanently win the right to veto?
cards.answer: Amsterdam is still a Wikimedia caching data centre, renamed esams. The veto is over the product: a MediaWiki feature too expensive to serve does not get enabled on Wikipedia, so personalisation is a cost the edge charges back to the origin.
cards.body: Wikitech still calls esams “a caching data center”, now inside Digital Realty's AMS9 — same city, same job, renamed along the way. The 2005 shape held. The price it set: personalisation became a budget line. Anything that makes a page differ per reader has to be paid for at the origin, forever.
